title: Mulligatawny
subtitle: Curried chicken and apple soup with rice and coconut cream
excerpt: Mulligatawny is the British-Indian soup that outlasted the empire: a spiced, slightly sweet chicken broth with diced apple, rice, and a finish of coconut cream. It arrived in Britain with returning colonial servants in the nineteenth century and became a staple of hotel dining rooms and pub kitchens for over a hundred years.
sourceNotes: Mulligatawny derives from the Tamil words for pepper-water (milagu-tannir). The soup was adapted heavily by British cooks in India during the colonial period, becoming a thick, curried chicken soup unrelated to its Tamil origins. It entered the British mainstream in the nineteenth century and remains in occasional use.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze without the rice. Defrost overnight and reheat gently with freshly cooked rice stirred in at serving.
recipe.batchNotes: Make a large batch and freeze in portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 3 days ahead without the rice. Add rice when reheating.

content.text: Mulligatawny is mild by Indian standards but confident in its own register: curry powder, sweet apple, coconut cream, and chicken together produce a soup that is warming and slightly exotic without being hot. The diced apple should hold its shape; cook it gently. The rice is served in the bowl, not cooked in the soup.

items.prepNote: peeled, cored, and diced (Cox or Bramley)

content.text: Heat a little oil in a large pan over medium heat. Cook {{onion}} chopped onion and {{carrot}} diced carrot for 8 minutes until soft. Add {{garlic}} crushed garlic, {{curry-powder}} of curry powder, and {{turmeric}} of turmeric. Cook for 2 minutes.

Add {{chicken-thighs-boneless}} diced chicken and stir to coat in the spices. Cook for 3 minutes. Add {{tomato-puree}} of tomato puree, the diced apple, and {{stock-chicken}} of stock. Simmer for 25 minutes.
Stir in {{coconut-cream}} of coconut cream and the lemon juice. Season with salt and pepper. Serve in deep bowls with a spoonful of cooked rice in the centre.

items.fix: Add more hot stock or water to reach a thin, broth-like consistency. Mulligatawny should pour easily, not plop.

items.cause: A Bramley apple was used and it cooked down to a puree, or it was added too early.
items.fix: Add the apple with the stock, not before. Cox or a firm eating apple will hold its shape better than Bramley.

items.cause: The curry powder was old or insufficient, and the lemon was omitted.
items.fix: Use fresh curry powder. The lemon juice brightens the whole dish and lifts the sweetness of the coconut.

items.symptom: The coconut cream has made the soup greasy
items.cause: The coconut cream was low quality or the soup was boiled after it was added.
items.fix: Add the coconut cream off the heat or at a very gentle simmer. Do not boil once it is in.

content.text: Mulligatawny was a fixture of British hotel and restaurant menus from Victorian times well into the twentieth century. It sits between British and Indian cooking and claims no authenticity in either. It produces a very good soup all the same. It is mild, warming, and slightly unusual: more interesting than plain chicken broth, with no specialist ingredients needed.
